attempts.raw_response: However, Uganda later withdrew from the joint venture and chose to route its crude oil exports southward through Tanzania to the port of Tanga instead. This decision left Kenya to pursue its own export infrastructure independently. Kenya subsequently shifted its focus to developing a standalone pipeline connecting the oilfields in the Turkana region to Lamu. Despite the setback, Kenyan officials maintained that the Lamu corridor remained the most viable export route for its crude. The government continued engaging international partners and investors to finance the project. Meanwhile, exploration activities in the South Lokichar Basin progressed, with early oil pilot production schemes designed to demonstrate commercial viability and attract further investment in the country's emerging upstream petroleum sector.

The route will remain as originally planned in the Uganda–Kenya Crude Oil Pipeline, in August 2015. The route, was proposed by Toyota Tsusho, the consultant selected by the two governments of that now-abandoned project.

Overview
Kenya has confirmed crude oil deposits of at least 750 million barrels. Originally Kenya partnered with Uganda to export that oil through a joint pipeline to Port Lamu on the Indian Ocean coast.
